## Analysis configuration

How much of the variation in median home value can four neighborhood
characteristics explain across Philadelphia? We fit four models to the same
1,720 block groups and compare their fit and the geographic structure left in
their residuals. Fujia Zheng completed the geographically weighted regression
and the final four-model comparison.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", out.width = "90%"
)

# rmarkdown renders relative to the directory containing this file.
project_root <- normalizePath("..")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project_root)

# Keep absolute image paths absolute. The report is knitted from code/ but
# written to ../output, so relative image paths are not found by pandoc.
options(knitr.graphics.rel_path = FALSE)

# Resolve every file in output/ from the project root, so the same path works
# for knitr (root.dir), for pandoc (absolute), and for a plain Rscript run.
out_path <- function(...) file.path(project_root, "output", ...)

model_formula <-
  LNMEDHVAL ~ PCTVACANT + PCTSINGLES + PCTBACHMOR + LNNBELPOV
```

## Packages

```{r packages}
required_part1 <- c("sf", "spdep", "lmtest")
required_part2 <- c("spatialreg", "ggplot2", "patchwork")
required_packages <- c(required_part1, required_part2)
missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Missing packages: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}

library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(lmtest)
library(spatialreg)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Data and model definition

The analysis uses 1,720 Philadelphia Census block groups. The dependent
variable is `LNMEDHVAL`, defined as `log(MEDHVAL + 1)`. The predictors are `PCTVACANT`, `PCTSINGLES`,
`PCTBACHMOR`, and `LNNBELPOV`. The latter is defined as
`log(NBelPov100 + 1)`.

The global spatial models and all residual Moran diagnostics use the same
row-standardized, first-order Queen weights in `data/RegressionData_queen.gal`.
For GWR, local estimation uses distances between block-group centroids.
The course shapefile does not identify its native coordinate reference system.
We matched all 1,720 course AREAKEY identifiers one-to-one to Census 2000
block groups, projected the matched polygons to NAD83 / UTM zone 18N
(EPSG:26918), and calculated centroids in metres. The additional 96 county
block groups in the reference file fall outside the course sample.
The original Queen graph is used for every residual comparison.
[U.S. Census Bureau boundary file](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2010/BG/2000/tl_2010_42101_bg00.zip)

```{r data-preview}
shapefile_path <- file.path(
  "data", "map_RegressionData", "RegressionData.shp"
)
shp_preview <- st_read(shapefile_path, quiet = TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(shp_preview) == 1720)

model_formula
st_drop_geometry(shp_preview)[1:6, c(
  "POLY_ID", "LNMEDHVAL", "PCTVACANT", "PCTSINGLES",
  "PCTBACHMOR", "LNNBELPOV"
)]
```

The project retains one shared Queen GAL file so the OLS residual checks,
Spatial Lag model, Spatial Error model, and GWR residual tests use the same
neighbor definition.

```{r run-part1, include=FALSE}

```

```{r queen-weights}
queen <- read.gal(
  file.path("data", "RegressionData_queen.gal"),
  region.id = as.character(shp_preview$POLY_ID)
)
queenlist <- nb2listw(queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

summary(card(queen))
sum(card(queen) == 0)
```

## Part 1 spatial autocorrelation and OLS

The reproducible Part 1 script performs the variable checks, global and local
Moran analyses, OLS diagnostics, weighted-residual regression, residual Moran
test, and handoff export.

### Global Moran's I for LNMEDHVAL

```{r response-moran-results}
read.csv(out_path("table_02_global_moran_lnmedhval.csv"))
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_01_moran_lnmedhval_scatter.png"),
  out_path("fig_02_moran_lnmedhval_permutation.png")
))
```

### Local Moran's I

The global statistic is 0.794 with a one-sided permutation p-value of 0.001.
Similar home values tend to cluster. At a local, unadjusted 5% threshold,
282 block groups form high–high clusters and 332 form low–low clusters.
Six are spatial outliers and 1,100 fall below the evidence threshold.
The local tests use 999 conditional permutations without replacement.

```{r lisa-results}
read.csv(out_path("table_03_lisa_cluster_counts.csv"))
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_03_lisa_significance_map.png"),
  out_path("fig_04_lisa_cluster_map.png")
))
```

### OLS regression and assumptions

```{r ols-results}
read.csv(out_path("table_04_ols_coefficients.csv"))
read.csv(out_path("table_05_ols_fit_statistics.csv"))
read.csv(out_path("table_06_ols_diagnostic_tests.csv"))

knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_05_ols_residuals_vs_fitted.png"),
  out_path("fig_06_ols_residual_histogram.png")
))
```

### Spatial autocorrelation in OLS residuals

OLS explains 66.2% of the variation in log median home value. Three
heteroscedasticity tests indicate unequal error variance, and the Jarque–Bera
test rejects normality. The residuals retain substantial spatial structure
(Moran’s I = 0.313, one-sided permutation p = 0.001). Neighboring block
groups tend to have prediction errors in the same direction.

```{r ols-residual-spatial-results}
read.csv(file.path(
  "output", "table_07_ols_residual_on_weighted_residual.csv"
))
read.csv(out_path("table_08_ols_residual_moran.csv"))

knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_07_ols_residual_vs_weighted_residual.png"),
  out_path("fig_08_ols_residual_moran_scatter.png"),
  out_path("fig_09_ols_residual_moran_permutation.png")
))
```

## Part 2 Model selection diagnostics

Both spatial models below are estimated on the same 1,720 block groups, the
same dependent variable, the same four predictors, and the same
row-standardized Queen weights as Part 1. The only thing that changes across
OLS, Spatial Lag, and Spatial Error is how spatial dependence enters the
equation, which makes the three sets of results directly comparable.

Before fitting either model, the Lagrange Multiplier tests applied to the OLS
residuals show which form of dependence dominates in this dataset.

```{r part2-run, include=FALSE}
source(
  file.path("code", "HW2_SL_SE_analysis.R"),
  local = knitr::knit_global()
)
```

```{r lm-diagnostics}
read.csv(out_path("table_09_lm_diagnostics_ols.csv"))
```

The plain LM statistics are both large, and the lag statistic
(`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(lm_rs$RSlag$statistic))`) is almost twice the error
statistic (`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(lm_rs$RSerr$statistic))`). The robust
versions settle the choice: robust LM lag stays highly significant
(`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(lm_rs$adjRSlag$statistic))`, p < 0.001), while robust
LM error collapses to
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(lm_rs$adjRSerr$statistic))` with
p = `r sprintf("%.3f", lm_rs$adjRSerr$p.value)`. In other words, once a lag term
is allowed for, the residuals do not add independent evidence of error
dependence. That points to the Spatial Lag model as the better specification,
but the Spatial Error model is estimated and reported as well because both are
part of the assignment and the two fit differently.

## Part 2 Spatial Lag regression

The Spatial Lag model adds a spatially lagged dependent variable to the OLS
specification:

$$y = X\beta + \rho Wy + \varepsilon$$

where $Wy$ is the row-standardized Queen average of `LNMEDHVAL` in the
neighbouring block groups and $\rho$ is the autoregressive coefficient on that
average. The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with `lagsarlm`, so the
coefficient standard errors account for the endogeneity that the lag term
introduces.

```{r sl-model-summary}
cat(readLines(out_path("sl_model_summary.txt")), sep = "\n")
```

```{r sl-coefficients}
read.csv(out_path("table_10_sl_coefficients.csv"))
```

```{r sl-fit-statistics}
read.csv(out_path("table_11_sl_fit_statistics.csv"))
```

### Spatial Lag residual diagnostics

```{r sl-diagnostics}
read.csv(out_path("table_12_sl_diagnostics.csv"))
```

```{r sl-residual-figures, out.width = "88%"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_10_sl_residual_map.png"),
  out_path("fig_11_sl_residual_moran_scatter.png"),
  out_path("fig_12_sl_residual_moran_permutation.png")
))
```

```{r sl-implied-mean, include=FALSE}
sl_xbar <- colMeans(model_data[, c("PCTVACANT", "PCTSINGLES",
                                   "PCTBACHMOR", "LNNBELPOV")])
sl_implied_mean <- (
  coef(sl)["(Intercept)"] + sum(coef(sl)[names(sl_xbar)] * sl_xbar)
) / (1 - sl_rho)
```

### Interpretation of the Spatial Lag model

The lag parameter is large and precisely estimated:
$\rho$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", sl_rho)` with a standard error of
`r sprintf("%.4f", sl_rho_se)` and a Wald z of
`r sprintf("%.2f", sl_rho_z)`, so a block group whose neighbours average one
unit higher on logged median house value is expected to sit about
`r sprintf("%.3f", sl_rho)` units higher itself, holding its own four
characteristics constant. Housing value in Philadelphia is therefore not only a
function of what is inside a block group; it is also a function of where the
block group sits.

All four predictors keep the same signs as in OLS, but their coefficients are
smaller: `PCTVACANT` moves from
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["PCTVACANT"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(sl)["PCTVACANT"])`, `PCTBACHMOR` from
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["PCTBACHMOR"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(sl)["PCTBACHMOR"])`, and `LNNBELPOV` from
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["LNNBELPOV"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(sl)["LNNBELPOV"])`. These are structural slope
parameters. Feedback between areas makes direct and indirect impacts depend
on the spatial multiplier. With these row-standardized weights, a uniform
one-unit increase across all areas gives a model-implied change of
$\beta/(1-\rho)$: about
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(sl)["PCTVACANT"] / (1 - sl_rho))` for `PCTVACANT` and
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(sl)["PCTBACHMOR"] / (1 - sl_rho))` for `PCTBACHMOR`.
Read that way, the substantive associations are not weaker than in OLS; the OLS
coefficients were mixing a block group's own attributes with those of its
neighbours. The much lower intercept
(`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(sl)["(Intercept)"])` instead of
`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(ols)["(Intercept)"])`) follows from the same mechanism:
with $\rho$ carrying the city-wide level, the constant no longer has to stand
for an average block group. If every block group had the sample-mean predictor
values, the model would give each one the same expected log value,
$(\alpha + \sum_k \beta_k \bar{x}_k)/(1-\rho)$, is
`r sprintf("%.2f", sl_implied_mean)`, against a sample mean of
`r sprintf("%.2f", mean(model_data$LNMEDHVAL))` for `LNMEDHVAL`.

The fit statistics confirm the improvement. The log likelihood rises from
`r sprintf("%.2f", ols_ll)` for OLS to `r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(logLik(sl)))`,
AIC falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", ols_aic)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(sl))`, and
the likelihood ratio test against OLS gives
`r sprintf("%.1f", unname(sl_lr$statistic))` on one degree of freedom
(p < 0.001). The Spatial Lag model is therefore a clear gain over the
independence model.

The residual diagnostics must be read as a mixed picture. The Breusch-Pagan
statistic is still `r sprintf("%.1f", unname(sl_bp$statistic))` (p < 0.001)
and the Koenker-Bassett version is still
`r sprintf("%.1f", unname(sl_kb$statistic))` (p < 0.001), so the lag term
absorbs dependence but not unequal error variance across block groups. The
Jarque-Bera statistic of `r sprintf("%.0f", unname(sl_jb$statistic))` says the
residuals remain heavy-tailed, which is expected given the extreme block
groups visible in the map. Inference in this model rests on the asymptotic
maximum-likelihood standard errors and should be read with that caveat.

The Spatial Lag fit reduces the magnitude of residual spatial association
and changes its direction. Its residual Moran's I is
`r sprintf("%.4f", sl_moran_i)`, versus
`r sprintf("%.4f", unname(ols_moran$statistic))` for OLS. The one-sided
permutation test for positive autocorrelation now gives p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", sl_moran_gt$p.value)`.
The two-sided test still detects the small negative value (p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", sl_moran$p.value)`). High and low errors tend to be adjacent
slightly more often than the random-permutation benchmark would suggest.

## Part 2 Spatial Error regression

The Spatial Error model leaves the regression equation in its OLS form but
allows the disturbance to be spatially correlated:

$$y = X\beta + u, \qquad u = \lambda Wu + \varepsilon$$

Here $\lambda$ is the autoregressive coefficient on the neighbour-averaged
error, that is, the model attributes spatial dependence to unobserved factors
that are shared among neighbouring block groups rather than to a spillover of
the dependent variable itself. It is estimated with `errorsarlm` under the
same maximum-likelihood framework.

```{r se-model-summary}
cat(readLines(out_path("se_model_summary.txt")), sep = "\n")
```

```{r se-coefficients}
read.csv(out_path("table_13_se_coefficients.csv"))
```

```{r se-fit-statistics}
read.csv(out_path("table_14_se_fit_statistics.csv"))
```

### Spatial Error residual diagnostics

```{r se-diagnostics}
read.csv(out_path("table_15_se_diagnostics.csv"))
```

```{r se-residual-figures, out.width = "88%"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  out_path("fig_13_se_residual_map.png"),
  out_path("fig_14_se_residual_moran_scatter.png"),
  out_path("fig_15_se_residual_moran_permutation.png")
))
```

### Interpretation of the Spatial Error model

The error parameter is strong: $\lambda$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", se_lambda)` with a
standard error of `r sprintf("%.4f", se_lambda_se)` and a Wald z of
`r sprintf("%.2f", se_lambda_z)`. A coefficient of that size means the
unexplained part of a block group's housing value tracks the unexplained part
of its neighbours' values. Shared, unmeasured neighborhood characteristics
are a possible explanation. Identifying a specific omitted factor would
require additional measurements.

The predictor coefficients keep the OLS signs but move substantially toward
zero: `PCTVACANT` from `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["PCTVACANT"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(se)["PCTVACANT"])`, `PCTBACHMOR` from
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["PCTBACHMOR"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(se)["PCTBACHMOR"])`, `LNNBELPOV` from
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(ols)["LNNBELPOV"])` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", coef(se)["LNNBELPOV"])`. The intercept, unlike in the Spatial
Lag model, stays close to the OLS value
(`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(se)["(Intercept)"])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(ols)["(Intercept)"])`), which is consistent with the
error specification keeping the global mean rather than shifting it into a lag
term. The shrinkage of the slopes is the substantive point: part of what looked
like an effect of vacancy or education in OLS was really the spatially
clustered context that both the predictor and the outcome share.

Against OLS the improvement is again decisive. Log likelihood
`r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(logLik(se)))` versus `r sprintf("%.2f", ols_ll)`,
AIC `r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(se))` versus `r sprintf("%.1f", ols_aic)`, and the
likelihood ratio test gives `r sprintf("%.1f", unname(se_lr$statistic))` on one
degree of freedom (p < 0.001). It is nevertheless weaker than the Spatial Lag
model on both criteria, which is discussed in the comparison below.

The residual picture is more comfortable than for the Spatial Lag model on the
heteroscedasticity side. The classical Breusch-Pagan statistic is
`r sprintf("%.2f", unname(se_bp$statistic))` (p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", se_bp$p.value)`), but the studentized Koenker-Bassett
statistic is only `r sprintf("%.2f", unname(se_kb$statistic))` with p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", se_kb$p.value)`, so the rejection of constant error
variance is much less robust here than under OLS or Spatial Lag. Normality still
fails (Jarque-Bera `r sprintf("%.0f", unname(se_jb$statistic))`, p < 0.001).

The Spatial Error residuals show a small negative spatial association.
Their Moran's I is
`r sprintf("%.4f", se_moran_i)` (one-sided p for positive autocorrelation =
`r sprintf("%.3f", se_moran_gt$p.value)`; two-sided p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", se_moran$p.value)`), against
`r sprintf("%.4f", unname(ols_moran$statistic))` for OLS. The error model also
overshoots slightly, and by a marginally larger margin than the lag model.

## Part 2 OLS, Spatial Lag and Spatial Error side by side

```{r part2-comparison}
read.csv(out_path("table_16_model_comparison_ols_sl_se.csv"))
```

Three things stand out. First, both spatial models beat OLS by an enormous
margin: AIC drops from `r sprintf("%.1f", ols_aic)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(sl))` (lag) and `r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(se))` (error), and
the likelihood ratio tests are overwhelming in both cases. Second, the Spatial
Lag model is the better of the two, with the higher log likelihood, the lower
AIC, and the robust LM diagnostics pointing the same way. Third, both models
leave essentially the same faint negative residual autocorrelation
(`r sprintf("%.3f", sl_moran_i)` versus `r sprintf("%.3f", se_moran_i)`, both
two-sided p = `r sprintf("%.3f", sl_moran$p.value)`), so the choice between them
does not hinge on residual autocorrelation.

Among the two global spatial specifications, the fit and robust LM results
favor Spatial Lag. The estimated association with neighboring home values
admits several explanations, including shared neighborhood conditions.
GWR allows the four slopes to vary across the city.

## Part 3 Geographically Weighted Regression

### Adaptive bandwidth and overall fit

Fujia Zheng fitted the same four-predictor model at each block group.
Each local fit gives larger weights to nearby observations. Its bandwidth
is the distance to the selected nearest-neighbor rank, so the physical
radius adapts to the density of block groups. The bandwidth search uses
the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc).

```{r part3-run, include=FALSE}
source(file.path("code", "HW2_GWR_analysis.R"), local = new.env(parent = knitr::knit_global()))
gwr_fit <- read.csv(out_path("table_18_gwr_fit.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
gwr_local <- read.csv(out_path("table_19_gwr_local_summary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
gwr_moran <- read.csv(out_path("table_20_gwr_moran.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
```

```{r gwr-fit-results}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Statistic = names(gwr_fit), Value = as.numeric(gwr_fit[1, ])),
             digits = 3, caption = "Adaptive GWR at the selected bandwidth")
```

### Local relationships and explanatory power

The AICc search selected the 14th nearest other block group. That neighbor
is typically 723 m away, ranging from 452 m to 3.72 km across the city.
More distant groups retain progressively smaller Gaussian weights.

The maps express local slopes in units of their estimated standard errors.
A negative ratio indicates a negative local association after adjustment for
the other three variables. Nearby estimates share observations, and scanning
1,720 locations entails multiple comparisons. Interpret the maps as
descriptions of geographic variation.

```{r gwr-local-results}
knitr::kable(gwr_local, digits = 3, caption = "Distribution of local regression results")
knitr::include_graphics(c(out_path("fig_16_gwr_coefficient_se.png"),
                          out_path("fig_17_gwr_local_r2.png")))
```

The bachelor's-degree coefficient is positive at all 1,720 locations. Its
median is 0.0189 in the westernmost quarter of sampled block groups and
0.0094 in the easternmost quarter. The singles coefficient even changes
direction, with a median of +0.0058 in the northernmost quarter and −0.0061 in
the southernmost quarter. These quarters are defined by centroid coordinates.
Vacancy and poverty have negative slopes in 1,550 and 1,442 groups,
respectively. Local R² ranges from 0.135 to 0.886, with a median of 0.634.
The spatial variation helps explain why a citywide slope can conceal
substantial neighborhood differences.

### Residual spatial dependence

```{r gwr-residual-results}
knitr::kable(gwr_moran, digits = 4, caption = "Queen-weight residual Moran diagnostics, 999 permutations")
knitr::include_graphics(c(out_path("fig_18_gwr_residual_map.png"),
                          out_path("fig_19_gwr_residual_moran.png")))
```

GWR residual Moran’s I is 0.0342 (one-sided p = 0.010, two-sided p = 0.020).
The remaining clustering is weak but detectable with the original Queen graph.

## Model comparison

We compare AIC on the same log-home-value outcome and all 1,720 observations.
The residual diagnostic asks a separate question: how much neighborhood
similarity remains after fitting? An absolute Moran's I closer to zero
indicates weaker global residual association under the shared Queen weights.

```{r final-model-comparison}
common <- read.csv(out_path("table_16_model_comparison_ols_sl_se.csv"))
four <- data.frame(
  Model = c(common$Model, "Adaptive GWR"),
  N = nrow(model_data),
  AIC = c(common$AIC, gwr_fit$AIC),
  AIC_course = c(common$AIC, gwr_fit$AIC_spgwr_eq4_22),
  Residual_I = c(common$Residual_Moran_I, gwr_moran$I),
  P_greater = c(common$Moran_p_greater, gwr_moran$P_greater),
  P_two_sided = c(common$Moran_p_two_sided, gwr_moran$P_two_sided)
)
four$Delta_AIC <- four$AIC - min(four$AIC)
write.csv(four, out_path("table_21_final_model_comparison.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(four, digits = 3, caption = "Model fit and residual spatial association")
```

Using the GWR AIC printed by the course's **spgwr** convention (equation
4.22), **GWR** has the lowest AIC (`r sprintf("%.2f", gwr_fit$AIC_spgwr_eq4_22)`) and the smallest absolute residual
Moran's I. The two AIC columns show why the penalty convention matters.
For GWR, the course statistic uses −2 log likelihood + tr(S), where tr(S)
is the effective number of fitted mean parameters. The other AIC column
uses −2 log likelihood + 2[tr(S) + 1], counting the variance parameter
and applying the usual Gaussian AIC penalty. AICc (`r sprintf("%.2f", gwr_fit$AICc)`) selected the
GWR bandwidth. [spgwr model documentation](https://rsbivand.github.io/spgwr/reference/gwr.html)

Under the common Gaussian AIC penalty the lowest AIC belongs to **`r four$Model[which.min(four$AIC)]`**
(`r sprintf("%.2f", min(four$AIC))`). **`r four$Model[which.min(abs(four$Residual_I))]`**
has the smallest absolute residual Moran's I
(`r sprintf("%.4f", min(abs(four$Residual_I)))`). OLS explains
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * summary(ols)$r.squared)` of the observed variation.
The corresponding in-sample quasi-global measure for GWR is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gwr_fit$R2)`. These fit statistics address
observations used in estimation. Prediction in previously unseen neighborhoods
would require a geographically held-out evaluation.
